claims.text: The material family of interest is multiphase refractory high-entropy alloys.
The primary mechanical property of interest is tensile ductility during aging.
CoCrFeNiTi is an example of a multiphase refractory high-entropy alloy.
The target alloys contain B2 or L12 chemically ordered nanoprecipitates.
The initial microstructure consists of a disordered solid-solution matrix containing fine, coherent, chemically ordered nanoprecipitates.
Rapid solidification or mechanical alloying forms the proposed coherent, chemically ordered nanoprecipitates.
Aging at 600–800 °C induces chemical ordering and precipitate evolution in the proposed alloys.
The alloys undergo a ductile-brittle-ductile transition during aging.
Coherent chemical ordering initially restricts dislocation motion and causes embrittlement.
Formation of coherent, chemically ordered precipitates increases stacking-fault energy.
Ordered precipitates create strong barriers to dislocation glide that lead to brittle fracture.
Precipitate coarsening reduces interfacial area and coherency strain.
Coarsening permits dislocation bypass through Orowan looping or precipitate shearing.
Loss of precipitate coherency and enhanced dislocation bypass restore ductility at later aging stages.
Elongation to failure first decreases and then increases with aging time.
The ductility minimum corresponds to peak chemical ordering and precipitate coherency.
Single-phase RHEAs and multiphase RHEAs without controlled ordering typically show monotonic ductility changes rather than a brittle intermediate state.
The transition requires a precipitate volume fraction high enough to embrittle the alloy but below the level causing immediate catastrophic failure.
The aging-temperature window must permit both ordering and coarsening kinetics.
The transition window depends strongly on alloy composition, ordering kinetics, and interference from phases such as sigma.

contradictions.description: The initial state is said to already contain chemically ordered nanoprecipitates, while aging and the early-aging mechanism are described as inducing or forming that ordering. The distinction between pre-existing ordering and aging-induced ordering is not defined.

The hypothesis associates recovery with higher aging temperatures, whereas the predicted curve and falsification experiment test recovery with aging time at a single temperature. These are different transition variables and are not reconciled.
